title: Book Five (1806 - 07) — Chapter 13
paragraphs: It was getting dark when Prince Andrew and Pierre drove up to the front entrance of the house at Bald Hills. As they approached, Prince Andrew pointed out with a smile a commotion at the back porch. A woman bent with age, a wallet on her back, and a short, long-haired young man in a black robe had dashed back to the gate on seeing the carriage. Two women ran out after them, and all four, glancing fearfully at the carriage, hurried up the steps of the back porch.

"Those are Mary's 'God's folk,'" said Prince Andrew. "They've mistaken us for my father. This is the one matter in which she disobeys him. He orders these pilgrims driven away, but she takes them in."
"But what are 'God's folk'?" asked Pierre.
Prince Andrew had no time to answer. The servants came out to greet them, and he asked where the old prince was and whether he was expected back soon.
The old prince had gone to town and was expected any minute.
Prince Andrew led Pierre to his own rooms — which were always kept in perfect order at his father's house — and went to the nursery.

"Let's go see my sister," he said to Pierre when he returned. "I haven't found her yet — she's hiding now, sitting with her 'God's folk.' It'll serve her right; she'll be embarrassed. But you'll see her 'God's folk.' It's really quite something."
"What are 'God's folk'?" asked Pierre.
"Come, and you'll see for yourself."

Princess Mary was indeed flustered, red patches appearing on her face, when they entered. In her cozy room, with lamps burning before the icon stand, a young man with a long nose and long hair, wearing a monk's cassock, sat on the sofa beside her, behind a samovar. Nearby in an armchair sat a thin, shriveled old woman with a meek expression on her childlike face.
"Andrew, why didn't you warn me?" said the princess, with mild reproach, as she stood before her pilgrims like a hen protecting her chicks.

"Delighted to see you. I'm very glad to see you," she said to Pierre as he kissed her hand. She had known him as a child, and now his friendship with Andrew, his marital troubles, and above all his kind, simple face inclined her warmly toward him. She looked at him with her beautiful, radiant eyes, and seemed to say: "I like you very much, but please don't make fun of my people." After the first greetings they sat down.
"Delighted to see you. I am very glad to see you."
"Ah, and Ivanushka is here too!" said Prince Andrew, glancing with a smile at the young pilgrim.
"Andrew!" said Princess Mary imploringly. "You must know that this is a woman," Prince Andrew said to Pierre.
"Andrew, for God's sake!" Princess Mary repeated.
"You must know that this is a woman."
"For heaven's sake."
It was clear that Prince Andrew's ironic attitude toward the pilgrims and Princess Mary's helpless attempts to shield them were their usual, long-established dynamic on this subject.
"But, my dear friend," said Prince Andrew, "on the contrary, you should be grateful that I'm explaining to Pierre your intimacy with this young man."
"But, my dear, you ought on the contrary to be grateful to me for explaining to Pierre your intimacy with this young man."

"Really?" said Pierre, peering over his spectacles with curiosity and seriousness — for which Princess Mary was especially grateful — at Ivanushka's face. Ivanushka, sensing she was being discussed, looked around at them all with sly eyes.

Princess Mary's embarrassment on behalf of her guests was quite unnecessary. They were not the least bit flustered. The old woman, eyes lowered but casting sideways glances at the newcomers, had turned her cup upside down and placed a nibbled piece of sugar beside it, sitting quietly in her armchair, clearly hoping for another cup of tea. Ivanushka, sipping from her saucer, watched the young men from under her brows with sly, feminine eyes.
"Where have you been? To Kiev?" Prince Andrew asked the old woman.

"I have, dear sir," she answered readily. "At Christmastime I was found worthy to receive the holy sacrament at the shrine of the saint. And now I've come from Kolyazin, sir, where a great and wonderful blessing has been revealed."
"And was Ivanushka with you?"
"I travel alone, kind sir," said Ivanushka, trying to speak in a bass voice. "I only ran into Pelageya at Yukhnovo."
Pelageya interrupted her companion — she obviously wanted to tell what she had seen.
"In Kolyazin, sir, a wonderful blessing has been revealed."
"What is it? Some new relics?" asked Prince Andrew.
"Andrew, please stop," said Princess Mary. "Don't tell him, Pelageya."

"No, why not, my dear? Why shouldn't I? I like him. He's kind, he's one of God's chosen, a benefactor — he once gave me ten rubles, I remember. When I was in Kiev, Holy Fool Cyril says to me — he's one of God's own, walks barefoot summer and winter — he says, 'Why aren't you going to the right place? Go to Kolyazin, where a miracle-working icon of the Holy Mother of God has been revealed.' Hearing those words, I said goodbye to the holy folk and went."
Everyone was silent; only the pilgrim woman went on in measured tones, drawing in her breath.
"So I come, sir, and the people say to me: 'A great blessing has been revealed — holy oil drips from the cheeks of our Blessed Mother, the Holy Virgin...'"
"All right, all right, you can tell us later," said Princess Mary, blushing.
"Let me ask her," said Pierre. "Did you see it yourself?"
"Oh yes, sir, I was found worthy. Such a brightness on the face, like the light of heaven, and from the Blessed Mother's cheek it drops and drops..."
"But my dear woman, that must be a fraud!" said Pierre naively, having listened attentively to the pilgrim.
"Oh sir! What are you saying?" exclaimed the horrified Pelageya, turning to Princess Mary for support.
"They're imposing on the people," Pierre repeated.

"Lord Jesus Christ!" cried the pilgrim, crossing herself. "Oh, don't say that, sir! There was a general who didn't believe — he said, 'The monks are cheating' — and the moment he said it, he went blind. And he dreamed that the Holy Virgin of the Kiev catacombs came to him and said, 'Believe in me and I will make you whole.' So he begged: 'Take me to her, take me to her.' It's the honest truth — I saw it with my own eyes. They brought him, quite blind, straight to her, and he falls down and says, 'Make me whole, and I'll give you what the Tsar gave me.' I saw it myself, sir — the star is set right into the icon. Well, and then what? He got his sight back! It's a sin to talk like that. God will punish you," she said admonishingly, turning to Pierre.
"How did the star get into the icon?" Pierre asked.
"And was the Holy Mother promoted to the rank of general?" said Prince Andrew with a smile.
Pelageya suddenly went very pale and clasped her hands.

"Oh sir, sir, what a sin! And you who have a son!" she began, her pallor flushing to vivid red. "Sir, what have you said? God forgive you! My dear, what does it mean?" she asked, turning to Princess Mary. She stood up and, nearly in tears, began gathering her things into her wallet. She was clearly frightened and ashamed to have accepted hospitality in a house where such things could be said, and at the same time sorry to lose the charity this house provided.
"Now, why did you have to do that?" said Princess Mary. "Why did you come to me?"

"Come, Pelageya, I was joking," said Pierre. "Princess, I give you my word, I didn't mean to offend her. I meant nothing — I was only joking," he said, smiling shyly and trying to make amends. "It was all my fault, and Andrew was only joking."
"Princess, on my word, I did not wish to offend her."
Pelageya hesitated, but Pierre's face showed such sincere penitence, and Prince Andrew looked so gently now at her and now at Pierre, that she was gradually reassured.

title: Book Five (1806 - 07) — Chapter 16
paragraphs: In April the troops were energized by news of the Emperor's arrival, but Rostov had no chance to attend the review at Bartenstein, as the Pavlograds were stationed at the outposts far from there.

They were bivouacking. Denisov and Rostov were living in an earth dugout that the soldiers had made for them, roofed with branches and turf. The dugout was built in the style that had become fashionable: a trench three and a half feet wide, nearly five feet deep, and eight feet long. At one end, steps were cut into the earth, forming the entrance and vestibule. The trench itself was the room, in which the lucky ones — like the squadron commander — had a plank laid on supports at the far end to serve as a table. On each side, the earth was cut back about two and a half feet, creating beds and couches. The roof was built so you could stand up in the middle and even sit up on the beds if you stayed close to the table. Denisov, who lived well because his soldiers liked him, also had a plank set into the roof at the far end with a piece of broken but mended glass for a window. When it was very cold, embers from the soldiers' campfire were placed on a bent sheet of iron on the steps in the "reception room" — as Denisov called that part of the dugout — and it became so warm that the officers, of whom there were always some visiting Denisov and Rostov, sat around in their shirtsleeves.

In April, Rostov was on orderly duty. One morning between seven and eight, returning after a sleepless night, he sent for embers, changed his rain-soaked underclothes, said his prayers, drank tea, warmed up, tidied the things on the table and in his corner, and then — his face glowing from the wind, wearing nothing but his shirt — lay on his back with his arms behind his head. He was pleasantly considering the likelihood of a promotion in a few days for his last scouting mission, and was waiting for Denisov, who had gone out somewhere and with whom he wanted to talk.
Suddenly he heard Denisov shouting behind the hut in an agitated, ringing voice. Rostov moved to the window to see who he was talking to and saw the quartermaster, Topchenko.
"I ordered you not to let them eat that Mashka root stuff!" Denisov was shouting. "And I saw with my own eyes how Lazarchuk brought some from the fields."
"I've given the order again and again, your honor, but they won't obey," answered the quartermaster.

Rostov lay back on his bed and thought contentedly: "Let him fuss and bustle — my job's done and I'm lying here. Perfect!" He could hear Lavrushka — Denisov's sly, bold orderly — talking with the quartermaster. Lavrushka was saying something about loaded wagons, biscuits, and oxen he'd seen when out looking for provisions.
Then Denisov's voice was heard shouting further and further away: "Saddle up! Second platoon!"
"Where are they off to now?" thought Rostov.

Five minutes later Denisov came into the hut, climbed with muddy boots onto the bed, lit his pipe, furiously scattered his things about, grabbed his weighted whip, buckled on his saber, and headed out again. When Rostov asked where he was going, he answered vaguely and irritably that he had some business to attend to.

"Let God and our great sovereign judge me afterward!" said Denisov as he went, and Rostov heard the hooves of several horses splashing through the mud. He didn't even bother to find out where Denisov had gone. Having gotten warm in his corner, he fell asleep and didn't leave the hut until evening. Denisov had not yet returned. The weather had cleared up, and near the next hut two officers and a cadet were playing a throwing game, laughing as their stakes buried themselves in the soft mud. Rostov joined them. In the middle of the game, the officers noticed some wagons approaching, with fifteen hussars on their gaunt horses riding behind. The wagons, escorted by the hussars, drew up at the picket ropes, and a crowd of hussars surrounded them.
"There — Denisov's been worrying," said Rostov, "and here are the provisions."
"So they are!" said the officers. "The soldiers will be thrilled!"
A little behind the hussars came Denisov, accompanied by two infantry officers with whom he was arguing.
Rostov went to meet them.
"I'm warning you, Captain," one of the officers — a short, thin man, obviously furious — was saying.
"Haven't I told you I won't give them up?" Denisov replied.
"You'll answer for this, Captain. It's mutiny — seizing your own army's transport. Our men haven't eaten in two days."
"And mine haven't eaten in two weeks," said Denisov.
"It's robbery! You'll answer for it, sir!" said the infantry officer, raising his voice.
"What are you pestering me for?" cried Denisov, suddenly losing his temper. "I'll answer for it, not you — and you'd better clear off before you get hurt. Go! Get out!" he shouted at the officers.
"Very well, then!" shouted the little officer, undaunted and not budging. "If you insist on robbing, I'll —"
"Go to the devil! Quick march, while you're still in one piece!" And Denisov turned his horse on the officer.
"Very well, very well!" muttered the officer threateningly, and turning his horse, he trotted away, bouncing in his saddle.
"A dog on a fence! A real dog on a fence!" shouted Denisov after him — the most insulting thing a cavalryman could say to a mounted infantryman — and riding up to Rostov, he burst out laughing.
"I seized those transports from the infantry by force!" he said. "After all, I can't let our men starve."

The wagons that had reached the hussars had been assigned to an infantry regiment, but when Lavrushka discovered the transport was unguarded, Denisov and his hussars had seized it by force. Biscuits were distributed freely to the soldiers, who even shared them with the other squadrons.
The next day the regimental commander sent for Denisov and, holding his fingers spread in front of his eyes, said:

"This is how I see the matter: I know nothing about it and won't open an investigation. But I advise you to ride to the staff and settle things in the commissariat department — if possible, sign a receipt for the supplies. Otherwise, since the demand was logged against an infantry regiment, there'll be trouble, and the affair could end badly."

From the regimental commander, Denisov rode straight to the staff, sincerely intending to follow this advice. That evening he returned to the dugout in a state Rostov had never seen him in before. Denisov couldn't speak — he was gasping for breath. When Rostov asked what was wrong, he could only manage some incoherent curses and threats in a hoarse, feeble voice.
Alarmed by Denisov's condition, Rostov suggested he undress, drink some water, and send for the doctor.
"Try me for robbery... oh! More water... Let them try me, but I'll always thrash scoundrels... and I'll tell the Emperor... Ice..." he muttered.
The regimental doctor, when he arrived, said bleeding was absolutely necessary. A deep saucer of black blood was drawn from Denisov's hairy arm, and only then could he tell what had happened.

"I get there," Denisov began. "'Where's your chief's office?' They pointed it out. 'Please wait.' 'I've ridden twenty miles and have duties — I can't wait. Announce me.' Very well — so out comes the chief himself, and he decides to lecture me: 'It's robbery!' 'Robbery,' I say, 'is not done by the man who seizes food to feed his soldiers, but by the man who takes it to fill his own pockets!' 'Be quiet!' 'Very well!' Then he says: 'Go give a receipt to the commissary, but your case will be referred to headquarters.' I go to the commissary. I walk in, and at the table — who do you think? No, wait! Who is it that's starving us?" shouted Denisov, slamming his fist on the table so hard it nearly broke and the glasses jumped. "Telyanin! 'What? So it's you who's been starving us? Take this! And this!' And I smashed him right in the face... 'Oh, you... you...' And I started thrashing him... Well, I had some fun, I can tell you!" cried Denisov, gleeful yet furious, his white teeth showing under his black mustache. "I'd have killed him if they hadn't dragged him away!"
"But what are you shouting for? Calm down," said Rostov. "You've opened up your arm again. Wait — let me rebandage it."
Denisov was bandaged up again and put to bed. The next day he woke up calm and cheerful.

But at noon the regimental adjutant came into Rostov and Denisov's dugout with a grave expression and regretfully showed them a document addressed to Major Denisov from the regimental commander, informing them of an inquiry into the previous day's events. The adjutant told them the affair was likely to take a very bad turn: a court-martial had been convened, and given the current severity against marauding and insubordination, demotion to the ranks would be the best Denisov could hope for.

The case, as presented by the complainants, was that Major Denisov, after seizing the transports while drunk, had gone to the chief quartermaster and without provocation called him a thief, threatened to strike him, and when led out had rushed into the office, beaten up two officials, and dislocated one's arm.

When Rostov pressed him with more questions, Denisov said with a laugh that he vaguely recalled some other fellow getting mixed up in it, but that it was all nonsense. He wasn't the least bit worried about any trial, and if those scoundrels dared come at him, he'd give them an answer they wouldn't soon forget.

Denisov talked about the whole thing with contempt, but Rostov knew him too well not to see that — while hiding it from everyone — he was genuinely afraid of the court-martial and worried about the case, which was clearly going badly. Every day brought letters of inquiry and notices from the court, and on the first of May, Denisov was ordered to hand his squadron over to the next in seniority and appear before his division's staff to explain his behavior at the commissariat office. The day before, Platov reconnoitered with two Cossack regiments and two squadrons of hussars. Denisov, as was his habit, rode out in front of the line, showing off his courage. A bullet from a French sharpshooter hit him in the fleshy part of his leg. At any other time Denisov would not have left the regiment for so minor a wound, but now he used it as an excuse to avoid the staff hearing and went to the hospital.

title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter 5
paragraphs: While waiting for his committee appointment, Prince Andrew looked up his old acquaintances, particularly those he knew to be in power and whose help he might need. In Petersburg he now felt what he had felt on the eve of battle: a troubled curiosity, an irresistible pull toward the ruling circles where the future — on which the fate of millions depended — was being shaped. From the irritation of older officials, the curiosity of outsiders, the discretion of insiders, the hurry and preoccupation of everyone, and the countless committees and commissions he heard about daily, he sensed that here in Petersburg in 1809, a vast civic battle was being prepared — one whose commander in chief was a mysterious figure he didn't know but who was said to be a genius: Speransky. And this reform movement, which Prince Andrew understood only vaguely, with Speransky as its chief driver, began to interest him so intensely that the question of army regulations quickly receded to second place in his mind.

Prince Andrew was ideally positioned to gain entry to the highest and most varied Petersburg circles. The reforming party welcomed and courted him — first because he was reputed to be clever and exceptionally well-read, and second because by freeing his serfs he had earned a reputation as a liberal. The old guard, who disapproved of the innovations, turned to him expecting sympathy, simply because he was his father's son. Fashionable society welcomed him gladly because he was rich, distinguished, a good match, and almost a newcomer with a halo of romance from his supposed death and the tragic loss of his wife. Besides all this, the general view of everyone who had known him before was that he had greatly improved over the past five years — softened, become more mature, lost his old affectation, pride, and contemptuous irony, and gained the calm that comes with age. People talked about him, were interested in him, and wanted to meet him.

The day after his interview with Arakcheev, Prince Andrew spent the evening at Count Kochubey's. He told the count about his meeting with "Sila Andreevich" — Kochubey used that nickname with the same vague irony Prince Andrew had noticed in the War Minister's waiting room.
"My dear friend, even in this matter you can't get by without Michael Mikhailovich Speransky. He manages everything. I'll speak to him. He's promised to come this evening."
"What does Speransky have to do with army regulations?" asked Prince Andrew.
Kochubey shook his head with a knowing smile, as if surprised by Bolkonski's naivety.
"We were talking about you with him just the other day," Kochubey continued, "and about your freed serfs."
"Oh, so it's you, Prince, who've freed your serfs?" said an old man of Catherine's era, turning contemptuously toward Bolkonski.
"It was a small estate that brought in no income," replied Prince Andrew, trying to downplay his action so as not to needlessly irritate the old man.
"Afraid of being late..." said the old man, glancing at Kochubey.

"There's one thing I don't understand," he went on. "Who will plow the land if they're set free? It's easy to write laws but hard to govern. It's the same as now — I ask you, Count — who'll run the departments when everyone has to pass examinations?"
"Those who pass the examinations, I suppose," replied Kochubey, crossing his legs and looking around.
"Well, I have Pryanichnikov serving under me — a splendid man, a priceless man — but he's sixty. Is he supposed to take an examination?"
"Yes, that's a difficulty, since education is not yet widespread, but..."

Count Kochubey didn't finish. He stood up, took Prince Andrew's arm, and went to meet a tall, bald, fair-haired man of about forty, with a large open forehead and a long face of unusual, peculiar whiteness, who was just entering. The newcomer wore a blue tailcoat with a cross on a ribbon around his neck and a star on his left breast. It was Speransky. Prince Andrew recognized him at once and felt a throb within him — as happens at critical moments of life. Whether it was respect, envy, or anticipation, he couldn't tell. Speransky's whole figure was of a distinctive type that made him instantly recognizable. In the society Prince Andrew frequented, he had never encountered anyone who combined such awkward, clumsy gestures with such calm self-possession; he had never seen such a resolute yet gentle expression as that in those half-closed, slightly moist eyes, or so firm a smile that expressed nothing in particular; nor had he heard such a refined, smooth, soft voice. Above all, he had never seen such delicate whiteness of face and hands — broad hands, but very plump, soft, and white. Such whiteness and softness Prince Andrew had only seen on the faces of soldiers who had been in the hospital a long time. This was Speransky, Secretary of State, the Emperor's constant companion and counselor at Erfurt, where he had met and talked with Napoleon on more than one occasion.

Speransky did not shift his gaze from face to face as people instinctively do when entering a large gathering, and was in no hurry to speak. He spoke slowly, confident he would be listened to, and looked only at the person he was addressing.

Prince Andrew followed Speransky's every word and gesture with particular attention. As sometimes happens — especially with people who judge those around them harshly — whenever he met someone new, especially someone he knew by reputation, like Speransky, he expected to discover in him the perfection of human qualities.

Speransky told Kochubey he was sorry he couldn't come sooner — he'd been held up at the palace. He didn't say the Emperor had detained him, and Prince Andrew noticed this affectation of modesty. When Kochubey introduced him, Speransky slowly turned his gaze to Bolkonski with his customary smile and looked at him in silence.
"I am very glad to make your acquaintance. I've heard of you, as everyone has," he said after a pause.
Kochubey said a few words about Arakcheev's reception of Bolkonski. Speransky smiled more noticeably.

"The chairman of the Army Regulations Committee is my good friend Monsieur Magnitsky," he said, fully articulating every word and syllable, "and if you like, I can put you in touch with him." He paused at the period. "I hope you will find him open-minded and ready to support everything reasonable."
A circle quickly formed around Speransky, and the old man who had talked about his subordinate Pryanichnikov addressed a question to him.

Prince Andrew, without joining the conversation, watched Speransky's every move — this man who not long ago had been an insignificant seminary student and now, Bolkonski thought, held in his plump white hands the fate of Russia. Prince Andrew was struck by the extraordinary disdainful composure with which Speransky answered the old man. He seemed to be addressing condescending words to him from an immeasurable height. When the old man started talking too loudly, Speransky smiled and said he couldn't judge the merits of what pleased the sovereign.
After chatting briefly in the general circle, Speransky rose and came up to Prince Andrew, taking him to the far end of the room. It was clear he thought it worth cultivating Bolkonski.

"I had no chance to talk with you, Prince, during that lively exchange the venerable gentleman drew me into," he said, with a slightly contemptuous smile that seemed to say: "You and I both understand how insignificant those people are." This flattered Prince Andrew. "I've known of you for some time — first from your liberation of your serfs, a pioneering example that deserves many more imitators, and second because you are one of those gentlemen of the chamber who have not taken offense at the new decree regarding court ranks, which is causing so much gossip and indignation."
"No," said Prince Andrew, "my father did not want me to take advantage of that privilege. I began my service from the lowest grade."
"Your father — a man of the previous century — evidently stands above our contemporaries who so condemn a measure that merely restores natural justice."

"I think, however, that these objections have some basis," said Prince Andrew, trying to resist Speransky's influence, which he was beginning to feel. He didn't want to agree with him on everything and felt a need to push back. Though he usually spoke easily and well, he found it hard to express himself now while talking with Speransky — he was too absorbed in studying the famous man's personality.
"Grounds of personal ambition, perhaps," Speransky said quietly.
"And of state interest, to some extent," said Prince Andrew.
"What do you mean?" asked Speransky softly, lowering his eyes.

"I am an admirer of Montesquieu," replied Prince Andrew, "and his idea that the principle of monarchies is honor strikes me as indisputable. Certain rights and privileges of the nobility seem to me a means of sustaining that sentiment."
"The principle of monarchies is honor seems to me incontestable. Certain rights and privileges for the aristocracy appear to me a means of maintaining that sentiment."
The smile vanished from Speransky's white face, which was much improved by the change. Apparently Prince Andrew's thought genuinely interested him.
"If you look at the question from that angle..." he began, pronouncing French with visible difficulty and speaking even more slowly than in Russian but quite calmly.
"If you regard the question from that point of view."

Speransky went on to say that honor — l'honneur — cannot be upheld by privileges that harm the state; that honor is either a negative concept of refraining from what is blameworthy, or it is a source of emulation in the pursuit of commendation and rewards. His arguments were concise, simple, and clear.

"An institution that upholds honor as a source of emulation — something like the Legion of Honor established by the great Emperor Napoleon — is not harmful but helpful to the success of the service, and is not a class or court privilege."

"I don't dispute that, but it cannot be denied that court privileges have served the same purpose," Prince Andrew responded. "Every courtier considers himself bound to maintain his position with dignity."

"Yet you yourself haven't chosen to avail yourself of the privilege, Prince," said Speransky, indicating by a smile that he wished to end amiably a discussion that was becoming uncomfortable for his companion. "If you would do me the honor of calling on Wednesday," he added, "I will have spoken with Magnitsky by then and can tell you what may interest you. I would also welcome the chance for a more extended conversation."
Closing his eyes, he gave a French-style bow without saying goodbye and, trying to draw as little attention as possible, left the room.

title: Book Seven (1810 - 11) — Chapter 10
paragraphs: "Does it ever happen to you," said Natasha to her brother when they had settled down in the sitting room, "does it ever happen that you feel as if nothing more is going to come — nothing — that everything good is already past? And not exactly bored, but sad?"

"Absolutely!" he said. "I've felt that way when everything was perfectly fine and everyone was cheerful. The thought would come to me that I was already tired of it all, and that we must all die. Once in the regiment I didn't go to some party where there was music... and suddenly I felt so low..."

"Oh yes, I know, I know, I know!" Natasha interrupted. "When I was little it used to happen to me. Remember when I was punished about those plums? You were all dancing, and I sat sobbing in the schoolroom? I'll never forget it — I felt sad and sorry for everyone, for myself and for everyone. And I was innocent — that was the main thing," said Natasha. "Do you remember?"

"I remember," answered Nicholas. "I remember coming to you afterward, wanting to comfort you — but, you know, I felt ashamed. We were terribly silly. I had a funny doll then and wanted to give it to you. Do you remember?"

"And do you remember," Natasha asked with a pensive smile, "how once, long, long ago, when we were quite small, Uncle called us into the study — that was in the old house — and it was dark — we went in and suddenly there stood..."
"A Black man," chimed in Nicholas with a smile of delight. "Of course I remember. Even now I don't know whether there really was a Black man, or if we only dreamed it or were told about it."
"He was gray, remember, and had white teeth, and he stood there looking at us..."
"Sonya, do you remember?" asked Nicholas.
"Yes, yes — I remember something too," Sonya answered timidly.
"You know, I've asked Papa and Mama about that man," said Natasha, "and they say there was no one at all. But you see — you remember!"
"Of course I do — I remember his teeth as if I'd just seen them."
"How strange it is! It's like a dream. I love that."
"And do you remember how we rolled hard-boiled eggs in the ballroom, and suddenly two old women started spinning around on the carpet? Was that real or not? Do you remember how funny it was?"
"Yes, and remember how Papa in his blue overcoat fired a gun on the porch?"

So they went through their memories, smiling with pleasure — not the sad memories of old age, but poetic, youthful ones, those impressions from one's most distant past where dreams and reality blend — and they laughed with quiet contentment.
Sonya, as always, couldn't quite keep pace with them, though they shared the same memories.
Much of what they remembered had slipped from her mind, and what she did recall didn't stir the same poetic feeling they experienced. She simply enjoyed their pleasure and tried to share in it.

She only truly participated when they recalled Sonya's first arrival. She told them how afraid she had been of Nicholas because he was wearing a braided jacket and her nurse had told her she too would be sewn up with braids.
"And I remember them saying you had been born under a cabbage," said Natasha. "I remember that I didn't dare not believe it, but I knew it wasn't true, and I felt so uncomfortable."
While they were talking, a maid poked her head in through the other door of the sitting room.
"They've brought the rooster, miss," she said in a whisper.
"It's not needed, Polya. Tell them to take it away," replied Natasha.
In the middle of their conversation, Dimmler came in and walked over to the harp standing in the corner. He removed its cloth covering, and the harp gave out a jarring sound.
"Mr. Dimmler, please play my favorite nocturne by Field," came the old countess's voice from the drawing room.
Dimmler struck a chord and, turning to Natasha, Nicholas, and Sonya, remarked: "How quiet you young people are!"
"Yes, we're philosophizing," said Natasha, glancing up for a moment, then continuing the conversation. They were now discussing dreams.

Dimmler began to play; Natasha tiptoed to the table, took a candle, carried it out, and returned, seating herself quietly in her former place. It was dark in the room, especially where they sat on the sofa, but through the large windows the silvery light of the full moon fell on the floor. Dimmler finished the piece but remained at the harp, softly running his fingers over the strings, clearly undecided whether to stop or play something else.

"Do you know," said Natasha in a whisper, moving closer to Nicholas and Sonya, "that when you keep going back and back through your memories, you finally start to remember things that happened before you were even born..."
"That's metempsychosis," said Sonya, who had always been a good student and remembered everything. "The Egyptians believed that our souls once lived in animals and will return to animals again."

"No, I don't believe we were ever in animals," said Natasha, still whispering even though the music had stopped. "But I'm certain we were angels somewhere up there, and we've been here before, and that's why we remember..."
"May I join you?" said Dimmler, who had come up quietly, and he sat down with them.
"If we were angels, why have we fallen lower?" said Nicholas. "No, that can't be!"

"Not lower — who said we were lower?... How do I know what I was before?" Natasha shot back with conviction. "The soul is immortal — well then, if I shall always live, I must have lived before, lived for a whole eternity."
"Yes, but it's hard for us to imagine eternity," remarked Dimmler, who had joined the young people with a mildly patronizing smile but now spoke as quietly and seriously as they did.
"Why is it hard to imagine eternity?" said Natasha. "It's today now, and it will be tomorrow, and always; and there was yesterday, and the day before..."
"Natasha! Your turn now. Sing something for me," called the countess. "Why are you sitting there like conspirators?"
"Mama, I really don't want to," replied Natasha, but she got up all the same.

None of them — not even the middle-aged Dimmler — wanted to break off their conversation and leave that corner of the sitting room. But Natasha stood up, and Nicholas sat down at the clavichord. Standing as she always did in the middle of the hall, choosing the spot with the best acoustics, Natasha began to sing her mother's favorite song.

She had said she didn't want to sing, but it had been a long time since she had sung, and a long time before she would sing again as she did that evening. The count, from his study where he was talking with Mitenka, heard her — and like a schoolboy rushing out to play, he stumbled over his words while giving orders to the steward and finally stopped, while Mitenka stood before him also listening and smiling. Nicholas didn't take his eyes off his sister and drew breath in time with her. Sonya, listening, thought of the vast difference between herself and her friend and how impossible it was for her to be anything like as captivating as her cousin. The old countess sat with a blissful yet sad smile and tears in her eyes, shaking her head now and then. She was thinking about Natasha and about her own youth, and about how there was something unnatural and frightening in this approaching marriage of Natasha and Prince Andrew.
Dimmler, who had seated himself beside the countess, listened with closed eyes.
"Ah, Countess," he said at last, "that is a European talent — she has nothing to learn. What softness, tenderness, and strength..."

"Ah, how afraid I am for her, how afraid!" said the countess, not realizing whom she was speaking to. Her maternal instinct told her that there was too much of something in Natasha and that because of this she would not be happy. Before Natasha had finished singing, fourteen-year-old Petya burst in excitedly to announce that mummers had arrived.
Natasha stopped abruptly.
"Idiot!" she screamed at her brother and, running to a chair, threw herself into it, sobbing so violently that she couldn't stop for a long time.
"It's nothing, Mama, really nothing — Petya just startled me," she said, trying to smile, but tears kept flowing and sobs still shook her.

The mummers — house serfs dressed up as bears, Turks, innkeepers, and fine ladies — frightening and funny, bringing with them the cold from outside and a feeling of gaiety, crowded at first timidly into the anteroom, then, hiding behind one another, pushed into the ballroom where, shyly at first and then more and more merrily and wholeheartedly, they began singing, dancing, and playing Christmas games. The countess, after identifying them and laughing at their costumes, went into the drawing room. The count sat in the ballroom, beaming and applauding. The young people had vanished.

Half an hour later there appeared among the other mummers: an old lady in a hooped skirt — Nicholas; a Turkish girl — Petya; a clown — Dimmler; a hussar — Natasha; and a Circassian — Sonya, with mustache and eyebrows drawn in burnt cork.

After the condescending surprise, the failure to recognize anyone, and the praise from the people who were not in costume, the young people decided that their outfits were so good they needed to be shown elsewhere.
Nicholas, who was eager to take them all for a ride in his troika since the roads were in splendid condition, proposed to bring about a dozen of the serf mummers and drive to "Uncle's."
"No, why bother the old fellow?" said the countess. "Besides, you wouldn't have room to turn around there. If you must go, go to the Melyukovs'."
Melyukova was a widow who lived with her family and their tutors and governesses three miles from the Rostovs.
"That's right, my dear," chimed in the old count, thoroughly enthused. "I'll dress up right away and go with them. I'll make Pashette's eyes pop."

But the countess wouldn't agree to his going; he'd had a bad leg for days. It was decided that the count must stay, but that if Louisa Ivanovna — Madame Schoss — would go with them, the young ladies could go to the Melyukovs'. Sonya, usually so timid and shy, begged Louisa Ivanovna more urgently than anyone not to refuse.

Sonya's costume was the best of all. Her mustache and eyebrows were extraordinarily becoming. Everyone said she looked very handsome, and she was in a spirited, energetic mood quite unlike her usual self. Some inner voice told her that tonight or never her fate would be decided, and in her male attire she seemed a completely different person. Louisa Ivanovna agreed to come, and within half an hour four troikas with large and small bells, their runners squeaking and whistling over the frozen snow, pulled up to the porch.

Natasha was the first to set the merry holiday mood, and this merriment, passing from one person to the next, grew stronger until it reached its peak when they all came out into the frost and got into the sleighs, talking, calling to one another, laughing, and shouting.

Two of the troikas were ordinary household sleighs; the third was the old count's, drawn by a trotter from the Orlov stud; the fourth was Nicholas's own, with a shaggy little black shaft horse. Nicholas, in his old-lady costume belted with a hussar overcoat, stood in the middle of his sleigh, reins in hand.

It was so light that he could see the moonlight reflected off the metal harness disks and off the eyes of the horses, who looked around nervously at the noisy party gathered under the shadow of the porch roof.
Natasha, Sonya, Madame Schoss, and two maids got into Nicholas's sleigh; Dimmler, his wife, and Petya into the old count's; and the rest of the mummers took the other two sleighs.
"You go first, Zakhar!" Nicholas shouted to his father's coachman, hoping for a chance to race past him.

The old count's troika, carrying Dimmler and his party, started forward with a squeak of runners as if freezing to the snow, its deep-toned bell clanging. The side horses, pressing against the shafts, sank into the dry, diamond-glinting snow and tossed it up.

Nicholas set off behind the first sleigh; behind him the others followed noisily, their runners squeaking. At first they drove at a steady trot along the narrow road. While they passed the garden the shadows of bare trees fell across the road, hiding the brilliant moonlight, but as soon as they were past the fence the snowy plain — bathed in moonlight and motionless — stretched out before them, glittering like diamonds and mottled with bluish shadows. Bang, bang! went the first sleigh over a rut in the frozen road, and each sleigh behind it jolted the same way, and rudely breaking the frost-bound stillness, the troikas began to fly along one after another.
"A hare's track — lots of tracks!" rang out Natasha's voice through the frost-bound air.
"How bright it is, Nicholas!" came Sonya's voice.

Nicholas glanced around at Sonya and bent down to see her face more closely. A quite new, sweet face with black eyebrows and a mustache peeked up at him from her sable fur — so close and yet so far away in the moonlight.
"That used to be Sonya," thought he, and looked at her more closely and smiled.
"What is it, Nicholas?"
"Nothing," he said, and turned back to the horses.

When they reached the beaten highway — polished by sleigh runners and rutted by rough-shod hooves, the marks of which shone in the moonlight — the horses began pulling at the reins of their own accord and picked up speed. The near horse arched its head, broke into a short canter, and tugged at its traces. The shaft horse swayed from side to side, flicking its ears as if asking: "Isn't it time to begin?" Ahead, already far in front, the deep bell of the lead sleigh rang out more and more distantly, and the black horses driven by Zakhar were clearly visible against the white snow. From that sleigh came shouts, laughter, and the mummers' voices.
"Gee up, my darlings!" shouted Nicholas, pulling the reins to one side and cracking the whip.

Only the sharper wind meeting them and the jerking of the side horses — pulling ever harder and quickening their gallop — showed how fast the troika was flying. Nicholas looked back. With screams, squeals, and cracking whips that sent even the shaft horses into a gallop, the other sleighs followed. The shaft horse swung steadily under the arch over its head, never thinking of slowing down, ready to put on more speed when asked.
Nicholas overtook the first sleigh. They were racing downhill and out across a broad, well-trodden track through a meadow near the river.

"Where are we?" he thought. "It must be the Kosoy meadow. But no — this is something I've never seen before. This isn't the Kosoy meadow or the Demkin hill, and heaven only knows what it is! It's something new and enchanted. Well, whatever it may be..." And shouting to his horses, he began to pass the first sleigh.
Zakhar held back his horses and turned his face — already covered with frost up to his eyebrows — toward them.
Nicholas gave his horses their head, and Zakhar, stretching out his arms, clicked his tongue and let his horses go.
"Now watch yourself, master!" he cried.

Faster and faster the two troikas flew side by side, and faster moved the galloping legs of the side horses. Nicholas began to pull ahead. Zakhar, keeping his arms stretched out, raised one hand with the reins.
"Not a chance, master!" he shouted.

Nicholas pushed all his horses into a gallop and flew past Zakhar. The horses sprayed the fine, dry snow into the faces of those in the sleigh — beside them sounded the quick jingling of bells, and they caught confused glimpses of swiftly moving legs and the shadow of the troika they were overtaking. The whistling of runners on snow and the shrieks of girls could be heard from different sides.
Checking his horses again, Nicholas looked around. They were still surrounded by the magic plain bathed in moonlight and spangled with stars.

"Zakhar is shouting that I should turn left — but why left?" thought Nicholas. "Are we getting to the Melyukovs'? Is this Melyukovka? Heaven only knows where we're going, and heaven knows what's happening to us — but it's very strange and wonderful, whatever it is." And he looked around in the sleigh.
"Look — his mustache and eyelashes are all white!" said one of the strange, pretty, unfamiliar people — the one with the fine eyebrows and mustache.
"I think this used to be Natasha," thought Nicholas, "and that was Madame Schoss — but maybe not. And this Circassian with the mustache I don't know, but I love her."
"Aren't you cold?" he asked.
They didn't answer but started laughing. Dimmler shouted something from the sleigh behind — probably something funny — but they couldn't make out what he said.
"Yes, yes!" some voices answered, laughing.

"But here was a fairy forest with black moving shadows and a glitter of diamonds and a flight of marble steps and the silver roofs of fairy buildings and the shrill cries of strange creatures. And if this really is Melyukovka, it is stranger still that we drove heaven knows where and have arrived at Melyukovka," thought Nicholas.
It really was Melyukovka, and maids and footmen with merry faces came running out onto the porch carrying candles.
"Who is it?" asked someone from the porch.
"The mummers from the count's. I know by the horses," replied several voices.

title: Book Eight (1811 - 12) — Chapter 5
paragraphs: Boris had not succeeded in making a wealthy match in Petersburg, so with the same goal in mind he came to Moscow. There he wavered between the two richest heiresses, Julie and Princess Mary. Though Princess Mary, despite her plainness, seemed more attractive to him than Julie, he felt awkward about courting her without knowing why. When they had last met on the old prince's name day, she had answered at random all his attempts at sentimental conversation, clearly not listening to what he was saying.
Julie, on the other hand, accepted his attentions readily, though in her own particular way.

She was twenty-seven. After the death of her brothers she had become very wealthy. She was by now decidedly plain, but thought herself not merely as good-looking as before but even far more attractive. She was confirmed in this delusion both by the fact that she had become a very wealthy heiress, and because the older she grew the less dangerous she became to men, and the more freely they could associate with her and take advantage of her suppers, parties, and the lively company that assembled at her house, without incurring any obligation. A man who ten years before would have been afraid of visiting daily where there was a seventeen-year-old girl, for fear of compromising her and committing himself, would now go boldly every day and treat her not as a marriageable girl but as a genderless acquaintance.

That winter the Kargins' house was the most pleasant and hospitable in Moscow. In addition to the formal evening and dinner parties, a large company, chiefly of men, gathered there every day, eating supper at midnight and staying till three in the morning. Julie never missed a ball, a promenade, or a play. Her dresses were always of the latest fashion. But despite all that, she seemed disillusioned about everything and told everyone that she didn't believe in friendship or love or any of the joys of life, and expected peace only "over there." She adopted the tone of one who has suffered a great disappointment, like a girl who has either lost the man she loved or been cruelly deceived by him. Though nothing of the kind had happened to her, she was regarded in that light, and had even herself come to believe that she had suffered much in life. This melancholy, which didn't prevent her from enjoying herself, didn't stop the young people who came to her house from having a good time. Every visitor paid tribute to the melancholy mood of their hostess, and then amused himself with society gossip, dancing, intellectual games, and rhyming games that were in fashion at the Kargins'. Only a few of these young men, among them Boris, entered more deeply into Julie's melancholy, and with these she had long private conversations about the vanity of all worldly things, and she showed them her albums filled with mournful sketches, maxims, and verses.

To Boris, Julie was especially gracious: she sympathized with his early disillusionment with life, offered him whatever consolation of friendship she — who had herself suffered so much — could give, and showed him her album. Boris sketched two trees in the album and wrote: "Rustic trees, your dark branches shed gloom and melancholy upon me."
On another page he drew a tomb, and wrote:
Death gives relief and death is peaceful. Ah! From suffering there is no other refuge.
Death gives relief and death is peaceful. Ah! From suffering there is no other refuge.
Julie said this was charming.

"There is something so enchanting in the smile of melancholy," she said to Boris, repeating word for word a passage she had copied from a book. "It is a ray of light in the darkness, a shade between sadness and despair, showing the possibility of consolation."
In reply Boris wrote these lines:

Poisonous nourishment of a too sensitive soul, Thou, without whom happiness would be impossible for me, Tender melancholy, ah, come and console me, Come calm the torments of my gloomy retreat, And mingle a secret sweetness with these tears that I feel flowing.

Poisonous nourishment of a too sensitive soul, Thou, without whom happiness would be impossible for me, Tender melancholy, ah, come and console me, Come calm the torments of my gloomy retreat, And mingle a secret sweetness with these tears that I feel flowing.

For Boris, Julie played the most mournful nocturnes on her harp. Boris read Poor Liza aloud to her, and more than once interrupted the reading because of the emotions that choked him. At large gatherings, Julie and Boris looked at each other as the only souls who understood one another in a world of indifferent people.

Anna Mikhaylovna, who often visited the Kargins, would play cards with the mother while carefully inquiring about Julie's dowry — she was to have two estates in Penza and the Nizhegorod forests. Anna Mikhaylovna regarded the refined sadness that united her son to the wealthy Julie with emotion and resignation to the Divine will.

"You are always charming and melancholy, my dear Julie," she said to the daughter. "Boris says his soul finds peace at your house. He has suffered so many disappointments and is so sensitive," said she to the mother. "Oh, my dear, I can't tell you how fond I've grown of Julie lately," she said to her son. "But who could help loving her? She is an angelic being! Oh, Boris, Boris!" — she paused. "And how I pity her mother," she went on; "today she showed me her accounts and letters from Penza (they have enormous estates there), and she, poor thing, has no one to help her, and they cheat her so!"

Boris smiled almost invisibly while listening to his mother. He laughed mildly at her naive scheming but listened to what she had to say, and sometimes questioned her carefully about the Penza and Nizhegorod estates.

Julie had long been expecting a proposal from her melancholy admirer and was ready to accept it; but some secret feeling of repulsion toward her, toward her desperate desire to get married, toward her artificiality, and a feeling of horror at giving up the possibility of real love, still held Boris back. His leave was running out. He spent every day and whole days at the Kargins', and every day on thinking it over told himself that he would propose tomorrow. But in Julie's presence, looking at her red face and chin (nearly always powdered), her moist eyes, and her expression of constant readiness to switch at once from melancholy to unnatural rapture at the prospect of married bliss, Boris could not bring himself to say the decisive words, though in his imagination he had long considered himself the owner of those Penza and Nizhegorod estates and had planned how to use the income from them. Julie saw Boris's indecision, and sometimes it occurred to her that she was repulsive to him, but her feminine self-deception immediately provided consolation, and she told herself that he was only shy from love. Her melancholy, however, began to turn into irritability, and not long before Boris's departure she formed a definite plan of action. Just as Boris's leave was running out, Anatole Kuragin appeared in Moscow, and naturally in the Kargins' drawing room, and Julie, suddenly dropping her melancholy, became cheerful and very attentive to Kuragin.

"My dear," said Anna Mikhaylovna to her son, "I know from a reliable source that Prince Vasili has sent his son to Moscow to get him married to Julie. I'm so fond of Julie that I'd be sorry for her. What do you think of it, my dear?"

The idea of being made a fool of and of having thrown away that whole month of painful melancholy service to Julie, and of seeing all the revenue from the Penza estates — which he had already mentally allocated and put to proper use — fall into the hands of another, and especially into the hands of that idiot Anatole, stung Boris. He drove to the Kargins' with the firm intention of proposing. Julie met him in a gay, careless manner, spoke casually of how she had enjoyed yesterday's ball, and asked when he was leaving. Though Boris had come intentionally to speak of his love and therefore meant to be tender, he began speaking irritably about how easily women can switch from sadness to joy, and how their moods depend solely on who happens to be paying court to them. Julie was offended and replied that it was true that a woman needs variety, and the same thing over and over again would bore anyone.

"Then I should advise you..." Boris began, wanting to sting her; but at that instant the galling thought occurred to him that he might have to leave Moscow without having achieved his aim, and have wasted his efforts for nothing — which was something he never allowed to happen.
He stopped himself in the middle of the sentence, lowered his eyes to avoid seeing her unpleasantly irritated and uncertain face, and said:
"I didn't come here to quarrel with you. On the contrary..."

He glanced at her to make sure he could go on. Her irritability had suddenly vanished, and her anxious, pleading eyes were fixed on him with greedy expectation. "I can always arrange not to see her often," thought Boris. "The thing has been started and must be finished!" He blushed deeply, raised his eyes to hers, and said:
"You know my feelings for you!"

There was no need to say more: Julie's face shone with triumph and self-satisfaction; but she forced Boris to say everything that's said on such occasions — that he loved her and had never loved any other woman more than her. She knew that for the Penza estates and Nizhegorod forests she could demand this, and she received what she demanded.

The engaged couple, no longer speaking of trees that shed gloom and melancholy upon them, planned the arrangements for a splendid house in Petersburg, paid visits, and prepared everything for a brilliant wedding.

title: Book Nine (1812) — Chapter 5
paragraphs: Davout was to Napoleon what Arakcheev was to Alexander — though not a coward like Arakcheev, he was equally precise, equally cruel, and equally unable to express his devotion to his sovereign except through cruelty.

In the organism of states such men are necessary, as wolves are necessary in the organism of nature, and they always exist, always appear and hold their ground, however incongruous their presence and proximity to the head of government may be. This inevitability alone can explain how the cruel Arakcheev, who tore out a grenadier's mustache with his own hands, whose weak nerves made him unable to face danger, and who was neither an educated man nor a courtier, was able to maintain his powerful position with Alexander, whose own character was chivalrous, noble, and gentle.

Balashev found Davout seated on a barrel in the shed of a peasant's hut, writing — he was auditing accounts. Better quarters could have been found for him, but Marshal Davout was one of those men who purposely put themselves in the most uncomfortable conditions to justify their being gloomy. For the same reason they are always hard at work and in a hurry. "How can I think about the bright side of life when, as you see, I'm sitting on a barrel and working in a dirty shed?" the expression on his face seemed to say. The chief pleasure and need of such men, when they encounter anyone who shows energy, is to display their own dreary, relentless activity. Davout indulged this pleasure when Balashev was brought in. He became still more absorbed in his work when the Russian general entered, and after glancing over his spectacles at Balashev's face — which was animated by the beauty of the morning and by his conversation with Murat — he did not rise or even stir, but scowled more deeply and sneered maliciously.
When he noticed the unpleasant impression this reception made on Balashev's face, Davout raised his head and coldly asked what he wanted.

Thinking he could only have been received this way because Davout didn't know that he was adjutant general to Emperor Alexander and even his envoy to Napoleon, Balashev hastened to state his rank and mission. Contrary to his expectation, Davout, after hearing him, became still surlier and ruder.
"Where is your dispatch?" he demanded. "Give it to me. I will send it to the Emperor."
Balashev replied that he had been ordered to hand it personally to the Emperor.
"Your Emperor's orders are obeyed in your army, but here," said Davout, "you must do as you're told."
And, as if to make the Russian general still more conscious of his helplessness before brute force, Davout sent an adjutant to call the officer on duty.

Balashev took out the packet containing the Emperor's letter and laid it on the table (made of a door with its hinges still attached, laid across two barrels). Davout took the packet and read the inscription.
"You are perfectly free to treat me with respect or not," protested Balashev, "but permit me to point out that I have the honor of being adjutant general to His Majesty..."
Davout glanced at him silently and clearly took pleasure in the signs of agitation and confusion on Balashev's face.
"You will be treated as is fitting," said he and, putting the packet in his pocket, left the shed.
A minute later the marshal's adjutant, de Castres, came in and took Balashev to the quarters assigned to him.
That day he dined with the marshal, at the same board on the barrels.

The next day Davout rode out early and, after calling for Balashev, bluntly ordered him to remain where he was, to move on with the baggage train if orders came for it to move, and to speak to no one except Monsieur de Castres.

After four days of solitude, boredom, and a painful sense of his own powerlessness and insignificance — particularly acute by contrast with the sphere of power in which he had so recently moved — and after several marches with the marshal's baggage and the French army, which occupied the whole district, Balashev was brought to Vilna — now occupied by the French — through the very gate by which he had left it four days earlier.
The next day the imperial gentleman-in-waiting, the Count de Turenne, came to Balashev and informed him of Emperor Napoleon's wish to honor him with an audience.

Four days before, sentinels of the Preobrazhensky regiment had stood in front of the house to which Balashev was conducted, and now two French grenadiers stood there in blue uniforms unbuttoned in front with shaggy caps on their heads, and an escort of hussars and Uhlans and a brilliant suite of aides-de-camp, pages, and generals, waiting for Napoleon to come out, were standing at the porch around his saddle horse and his Mameluke, Rustan. Napoleon received Balashev in the very house in Vilna from which Alexander had dispatched him on his mission.
